what_it_does: Computing-in-memory (doing math inside the memory chip rather than shipping data to a separate processor) is attractive for AI inference on low-power edge devices, but choosing the right memory technology involves trade-offs: fast volatile memory (like SRAM — fast-access temporary storage) draws continuous power even when idle, while non-volatile memory (like MRAM or ReRAM — which retain data without power) saves energy but can be slower or mismatched to workload demand. HH-PIM combines two heterogeneous (differently configured) compute modules — one tuned for high performance, one tuned for low power — both built from a mix of MRAM and SRAM. A runtime algorithm monitors the incoming AI workload and dynamically routes data to whichever module best matches the current computational demand, balancing energy and latency.
